assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, turned precision spectroscopy into a many-atom, quantum-limited measurement tool. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 test fundamental physics, enable relativistic geodesy and underpin a possible redefinition of the second. This is the kind of precision atomic physics where theory and experiment agree and the result is robust.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Ye's group drove the strontium clock to the performance frontier and the many-body and comb-linked clock work. A two-person prize is clean. Other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Schmidt, Hinkley/Ludlow at NIST) are not credited, so there is some credit-boundary risk, and the optical-comb side was already recognised in 2005.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently in many laboratories worldwide over roughly two decades, with clock comparisons and international frequency-ratio campaigns. Recognition would be timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to separate lattice-clock concept from ion-clock and comb contributions already honoured or deserving of recognition.
I cannot independently verify the latest stated uncertainty figures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes matter-wave coherence a precision instrument: gravimetry, gradiometry, measurement of G and the fine-structure constant, tests of the equivalence principle. It demonstrates that quantum mechanics operates on whole atoms across metre-scale separations and times, a fundamental point about the quantum-classical boundary.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, theory of atom-light interferometry), Pritchard (first atom interferometer with gratings, 1991) and Kasevich (laser-pulse interferometer, precision gravimetry, large-momentum-transfer devices) each have decisive early contributions. Müller is a younger leader of precision applications; leaving him out is defensible. Chu's related work was already honoured in 1997, which complicates the credit narrative.
assessment.maturity: Mature: decades of independent confirmation by many groups and operating devices in metrology and fundamental-physics tests. The strongest discoveries claims (equivalence-principle tests at ultimate precision) are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 prize for laser cooling and with Ramsey's separated-field methods.
Priority among the early 1991 demonstrations (Pritchard, Mlynek, Siu, Kasevich-Chu) is shared among several groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry phase show that potentials and geometry have physical meaning in quantum mechanics, not only forces and energies. They underlie much of modern physics, from molecular dynamics and conical intersections to the quantum Hall effect and topological matter. This is deep and unexpected conceptual physics of the kind I value.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) and Berry (1984) are the principal figures, but Bohm is deceased, and Ehrenberg-Siday (1949), Pancharatnam and Mead-Truhlar are precursors, so the prize would cut across a lineage. The two named people would honour two related but distinct discoveries, which is a loose single-topic definition.
assessment.maturity: The effects are confirmed beyond doubt (Tonomura electron holography, many solid-state and optical experiments). Recognition is long overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as one discovery or two, and whether the Aharonov-Bohm experimental confirmation needs separate credit.
Bohm's death and the prior-art claims weaken a clean attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, showing the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy and fermionic Mott and antiferromagnetic correlations. This opens controlled quantum many-body physics as a laboratory field and ties atomic physics to condensed-matter questions.
assessment.attribution: The experimental trio of Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger gives a coherent set (Mott transition with Hansch and Bloch, quantum gas microscope, Fermi-Hubbard realisation). Cirac and Zoller proposed the theoretical foundations (Jaksch et al.), so Zoller, Jaksch and Cirac have a legitimate claim; Jaksch is not credited here. Including theory would require dropping an experimentalist.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and widely reproduced for 20 years. Quantum-simulation claims about genuinely new regimes (for example the doped Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram) are still open.
uncertainties: Experiment versus theory allocation between Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller or Cirac.
Greiner's role overlaps with the Mott-transition work from the Munich group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Corkum's three-step recollision model and Lewenstein's quantum-mechanical strong-field theory explain high-harmonic generation, above-threshold ionisation and the attosecond pulse generation that the 2023 prize relied on. The picture is simple, physical and predictive, and it supports molecular orbital tomography and attosecond spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's semi-classical model (1993) is the decisive conceptual step; Lewenstein et al. (1994) gave the quantum theory. A third credit would typically go to Kulander, Schafer or Krause, who are not listed. I have collaborated closely with the attosecond community and with the 2023 laureate and should flag possible bias in judging closeness to that prize.
assessment.maturity: The model has been tested extensively in many labs and is the standard textbook framework. But the 2023 prize already recognised the experimental attosecond breakthrough, so the committee may regard this as a completion rather than a new discovery.
uncertainties: Is the discovery sufficiently distinct from the 2023 prize, or would the committee judge it as largely recognised?
Credit boundary with Kulander and Schafer.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 by ATLAS and CMS confirmed the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking and completed the Standard Model. The measurement is a landmark of large-collaboration experimental physics.
assessment.attribution: Individual credit is difficult: four people are credited and the Nobel limit is three. Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at the discovery), Della Negra and Jenni (ATLAS and CMS founders) and Virdee (CMS) represent leadership of the experiments rather than a single decisive insight. The scientific credit is spread across thousands of authors, and the theory was already honoured in 2013. I defer to colleagues in particle physics on this.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by two independent experiments and extended by the LHC Run 2 and 3 coupling measurements. Recognition would be mature, though the 2013 prize partly covered the discovery.
uncertainties: Which three of four to select; my choice of Gianotti, Della Negra and Virdee is not strongly grounded.
Whether the committee wants to recognise collaboration leadership.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light reduces quantum noise below the shot-noise limit, and its implementation in gravitational-wave interferometers is a direct application of quantum optics to a fundamental measurement. It illustrates how basic quantum-state engineering becomes precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-state interferometry (1981), Kimble led early observation of squeezing in cavity QED and later optical systems, and Schnabel led implementation in GEO600 and related work. Slusher, Wu and Kimble's 1985-87 experiments and Walls, Yuen and Mavalvala contributions complicate the credit.
assessment.maturity: Operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and widely reproduced. Maturity is good, but the largest impact came through the gravitational-wave detections recognised in 2017.
uncertainties: Several experimental groups from the 1980s are not included in the credited list.
The principal impact is in an apparatus already recognised by the 2017 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics demonstrates strong coupling of artificial atoms to photons in microwave resonators and gives the architecture for superconducting qubits, dispersive readout and quantum-state control. It is a clean, fundamental realisation of cavity QED in a solid-state system.
assessment.attribution: Blais proposed the architecture, Wallraff (with Schoelkopf's group at Yale) observed strong coupling in 2004, and Schoelkopf developed transmon and readout. A three-person prize is coherent, but Devoret, Martinis and Nakamura have a close relationship and the 2025 prize recognised related work, which creates a recent-overlap risk.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories and now the basis of commercial quantum processors. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes another circuit-quantum award less likely so soon.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and the question of whether this is distinct enough.
Ranking relative to cavity-QED work by Haroche, whose prize was in 2012.
